mappings.note: MCQ whose answer is the bare fact that only 70 of 100 pesos arrived. Retrieval, so LO-1; the long-answer version that asks about his state of mind is mapped to LO-2.
Asks the meaning of 'crest' as used in the line - a vocabulary item, which sits under C-E1.1, not under any literature outcome.
The postmaster framing the collection as 'an act of charity' is a statement about his character; not LO-1, because the point is his disposition rather than the event.
'How far would you agree' is an evaluation prompt answered from the learner's own reasoning, with no return to the text, so C-E1.2 and not a C-E1.4 outcome.
Asks the learner to judge whether Lencho's approach was justified and defend that judgement - opinion and reasoning (C-E1.2), not the character description that LO-2 would cover.
Two retrievable facts (who read the letter, what he did next). LO-1 rather than LO-2, since no motive has to be argued.
The behaviour of the family after the ruin is context and minor-character analysis, so LO-2; LO-1 would fit only a single stated fact.
Reads a quoted line for what it implies about farmers of that place and time - the 'context' half of LO-2, not simple extraction.
Composing a dialogue between Lencho and his wife is creative writing judged on style, tone and dialogue format, which is exactly C-E1.2; nothing is being extracted from the text.
'Elaborate with reference to A Letter to God' requires the answer to be built on textual evidence, which is what LO-3 names; LO-2 alone would miss the evidence requirement.
Core task is a character sketch of Lencho (LO-2); the alternative wording adds 'is such faith possible today', which is an opinion, hence the second code.
A chain of retrieval questions covering the letter, its recipient and his response - information from the prose, so LO-1 rather than the evaluative outcomes.
Write a personal letter in the postmaster's voice: role, tone and letter format are what is marked, which C-E1.2 names explicitly; the text supplies only the situation.
Both parts ask for the learner's own view and a first-person account as an employee. Personal opinion and perspective writing, not analysis of the given text.
Two prose extracts are supplied and the task is to compare the kind of help each character got - thematic reading of extracts, which is LO-1's territory.
Names the postmaster's values (character, LO-2) and then asks which the learner would emulate, a personal judgement (C-E1.2). Not LO-1: nothing is merely retrieved.
'Prove your point by giving examples from the text' is the textual-evidence outcome LO-3; the 'was he justified' framing adds the evaluative C-E1.2.

Extract-based item whose key sub-question asks which option uses the same kind of figurative comparison as 'these aren't raindrops, they're new coins'. Figures of speech are covered only by the C-E1.4 competency.
'According to the extract' - the answer is lifted from the supplied passage. LO-1, even though the content concerns belief, because no independent character analysis is asked for.
Retrieval of what the postmaster found he needed (more than goodwill, ink and paper). Straight extraction, so LO-1.
Lencho's unshaken confidence and his reaction on opening the envelope are character, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
'How do you know' forces the answer to cite what the story shows. That evidence demand is LO-3; LO-2 would cover only naming the trait.
The answer is the set of described actions (wrinkled brow, stamp affixed with a blow of the fist) - detail retrieval, so LO-1, not an argument about his character.
Effect of the hailstorm on the field is stated in the prose; pure extraction.
When and how the letter reached him - narrative facts. LO-1 rather than LO-2, since 'reaction' here is just the recorded anger, not an analysis.
Reproduces the content of Lencho's first letter as written in the story - extraction of information from the prose.
'Do you think' invites the learner to reject Lencho's verdict and defend the employees - an opinion with reasons, so C-E1.2, not the retrieval outcome.
The postmaster's reason for replying is his motive and the writer's point about protecting faith - LO-2, not the event itself.
Explaining the story's irony is applying a literary convention; no LO in this frame names devices, so the competency is the most specific legal code.
Retrieves the postmaster's plan and the steps he took to carry it out - a sequence of stated events, hence LO-1.
Poem item ('Dust of Snow'): the speaker's rueful mood before the snow fell is the persona's state, so LO-2. LO-1 is restricted to prose extracts and does not apply to the poem.
Asks for a reasoned opinion on whether Frost shows a cheerful side of nature. Judgement with justification, so C-E1.2 rather than a comprehension outcome.
Recall of the poem's situation (under the hemlock, a crow shakes down the snow). C-E1.4 covers recalling in verse; LO-1 is worded for prose extracts only.
Crow and hemlock as symbols of the bleak side of nature - symbolism is a literary convention, which only C-E1.4 covers.
Asks why the poet chose such unpoetic images - that is the writer's message and intent, named in LO-2, rather than just identifying the symbol as the sibling item does.
Tracks the emotions projected by the speaker across the poem - persona and context analysis, LO-2.
Names the unusual creatures Frost uses and what they stand for - recall plus symbolism, both inside the C-E1.4 competency and outside every LO.
Compares the thematic role of the crow and the seagull across a poem and a story - the writers' messages, LO-2. LO-1 is prose-only and this spans verse.
An imagined 120-word conversation between Frost and Lencho: creative composition with a word limit and a set opening line, judged on style and format.
Tests recall of the writer's coin image for the large raindrops - recognition of the figure, which sits in C-E1.4 and not in any of the three LOs.
